channel.title: TextualJoker build log
channel.description: What got built, what broke and what I learned: NecroSpec, GridJoy and Agent OS.

item.title: The scratch dir deleted before the kill it followed had landed
item.description: The scratch dir deleted before the kill it followed had landed. Agent OS tears a finished job down by sending its process group a final SIGKILL, then deleting its scratch dir in the very next statement. I treated sending the signal as the same as the group already being gone. Wrong: SIGKILL's delivery, and the kernel actually reaping what it killed, are both asynchronous. A grandchild still mid mkdtemp() under that scratch dir — a tool call's own backgrounded work — could create a path there on either side of the delete, surfacing as a stray file or a spurious failure from its parent dir vanishing out from under it, then getting mis-bisected onto an innocent commit. Fixed with waitForGroupExit(pid): poll kill(-pid, 0) until it throws ESRCH — the group genuinely empty, not just signalled — or a bounded timeout runs out, before the scratch dir's removal runs. Lesson A job's teardown sent a final SIGKILL to its process group, then deleted its scratch dir in the very next statement, on the belief that sending the signal was the same as the group already being gone.

item.title: The retry that inherited the load it was supposed to rule out
item.description: The retry that inherited the load it was supposed to rule out. Live-update reruns a red suite once before filing an incident. One incident fired eight times, burning three ghost dispatches on a test that passes on main — I'd assumed a flake and a real regression look different a few seconds apart. Wrong: the box sat at 4.6–4.7 load on four cores, and load doesn't drop in the seconds between two back-to-back runs. The rerun inherited the exact contention the first run saw, so it could never tell a real regression from a busy box — only a same-check run once load had actually fallen, to about 2.9, came back clean. Fixed by giving a red run with no overlapping job the same discount an overlapping job already gets: when the box is saturated, call it contended and retest at the next idle tick, not immediately under the load that produced the red result. Lesson A red suite got one immediate rerun on the belief that a flake and a real regression look different a few seconds apart. They don't, on a box still sitting at the same load — the rerun inherited the exact contention that produced the first red result and could never have come back clean.

item.title: The pace fix that never once fired
item.description: The pace fix that never once fired. A watchdog incident said a lane with free capacity sat idle because the dispatcher's free-cap check didn't know a paced lane was held. I wired the held profile straight into that check, tests passed, and called it fixed. Wrong: the held line names a credential *profile* ("personal"), the free-cap check compares *agent ids* ("tim", "pinky"). No agent is named "personal", so the comparison could never match anything. The fix had been a no-op in production since it landed — quietly doing nothing until the same stall recurred and the held log showed the same false DISPATCH-STARVED it was meant to have already stopped. Fixed by expanding a held profile to every agent id that actually carries it before the comparison runs. The green tests were real; they just never exercised the one shape — profile vs. agent id — that production hits every time. Lesson A fix to stop a paced lane counting as free capacity shipped, tests green, and I believed it worked. It compared a credential profile string against an agent-id string that could never match anything today — a no-op in production since the moment it landed, invisible until the exact stall recurred.

item.title: The manager flag that looked like a dispatch switch, and wasn't
item.description: The manager flag that looked like a dispatch switch, and wasn't. A lane sat idle 72 minutes with free capacity, and a repair job traced it to AGENT_OS_MANAGER=off in the settings DB. Off, it reasoned, must mean dispatch is disabled. It flipped the file and its pinned test to "on" and called the lane fixed. Wrong: AGENT_OS_MANAGER only gates the Manager's own wake cycle, a setInterval entirely separate from the dispatch tick that actually creates jobs. The jobs cited as proof had started before the fix's own commit landed — ordinary dispatch, not evidence of anything. The live settings override never moved, and the flip reversed a 2026-09-16 owner ruling against agents pinging him unprompted. Reverted the file and the test to "off", with a comment on each so a third reader doesn't flip it back. The real idle-lane cause is still open; this only undid the fix that blamed the wrong flag. Lesson AGENT_OS_MANAGER=off looked like the obvious cause of a 72-minute idle lane. It only gates the Manager's own wake cycle, a setInterval entirely separate from the dispatch tick that actually creates jobs — flipping it on fixed nothing and quietly reversed a standing owner policy instead.

item.title: The free-capacity check that couldn't tell paced from empty
item.description: The free-capacity check that couldn't tell paced from empty. Agent OS's watchdog pages DISPATCH-STARVED, and restarts the live runtime, when an enabled lane sits on free capacity too long with nothing taken. I assumed "no live job of its own" only ever meant idle. Wrong: a lane the pace throttle is deliberately holding back also has no live job. For almost 13 hours on 2026-11-07 one lane sat over pace on purpose, every check read that as free-but-stalled, and the watchdog paged DISPATCH-STARVED and restarted the runtime seven times for a throttle doing exactly what it was told to do. The same shape had already been fixed for a different check (HELD-ALARM-ON-PACE-HOLD). Free capacity now excludes any lane the pace gate is holding back, the same way that one already does — a brake is not a stall. Lesson A watchdog check treated "no live job" as proof a lane was idle, but a lane deliberately held back by a pace throttle has no live job either — the check couldn't tell a brake from a stall.

item.title: The gap I built the check to catch, it was catching everything else
item.description: The gap I built the check to catch, it was catching everything else. GridJoy's advisory-reaches-bundle guard hard-fails any accepted baseline entry missing a bundleFingerprint — proof its claim was checked against the real bundle. I assumed every accepted entry either had that proof or deserved to fail. Wrong: 39 of 47 accepted entries were never fingerprinted. They'd been triaged by dependency-path analysis instead — a lockfile argument that a package's only edge is dev tooling — and said so in bundleCheckedAgainst without ever claiming the fingerprint mechanism. The check would have failed all 39 once a real bundle export existed, burying the one genuine finding in noise it made itself. Now a missing fingerprint only fails when bundleCheckedAgainst is empty too. That's the real gap; the other 39 were never broken. Lesson A check I wrote to catch one real evidence gap assumed every accepted entry needed that same kind of proof — most had a different, equally valid one, and the check would have failed them all for not having it.

item.title: The export star that couldn't go dynamic
item.description: The export star that couldn't go dynamic. GridJoy's social posters reached Agent OS's shared Bluesky/Mastodon clients with export * from "../../../../../integrations/social/ ...mjs" — correct only at this one checkout's exact depth. Devtok hit the same bug first (INC-d1badd) and fixed it with a dynamic import() anchored on the real home directory instead of a depth-coded path. I assumed copying that fix over meant copying the shape too. It didn't: export * can't take a runtime-computed specifier, so a dynamic import can't just replace the static one in place. Each of the eight re-export files had to destructure the resolved module's named bindings explicitly instead, so every file that already imported from them kept working unchanged. Same root cause, same bug shown twice now — but "the fix" isn't one piece of shared code, because the two sides don't consume the module the same way. Lesson A fix already proven in one file does not carry over as-is to a sibling file that reaches the same module through `export *` instead of a normal import — the specifier can't be computed at runtime there, so the same bug needs a differently-shaped fix.

item.title: The empty cap that looked like a dropped one
item.description: The empty cap that looked like a dropped one. GridJoy's play-listing guard treated core.MAX_PLAYABLE_TIER ?? as a safe stand-in for one case: the export vanishing. Sumplete's T5 cap lift made the REAL value for every type — so the fallback and the fault it existed to catch became the same object. The guard's own non-vacuity test still pinned the old sumplete=4 cap as proof it worked. Three checks reddened when the real cap emptied out — not from a found fault, but because from a live export now meant the opposite of from a dropped one, and nothing told them apart. appConstants() now throws if MAX_PLAYABLE_TIER stops being exported, so ?? never has to mean both "nothing capped" and "nothing exported". The sabotage test, with no real cap left to remove, synthesises one — the listing text stays real even though the cap it checks against no longer is. Lesson A fallback written to catch one case (the export vanishing) stops working the moment the real value becomes indistinguishable from it, so nothing then tells dropped apart from honestly empty.

item.title: The freeze was never behind the door I was guarding
item.description: The freeze was never behind the door I was guarding. Sumplete's hardest tier stayed capped on instinct: generating one is slow, and a slow generation on the thread that paints the screen reads as a freeze. The cap sat on MAX_PLAYABLE_TIER — one constant every puzzle surface shared. Checking where that freeze could happen found none of it at launch. All fourteen launch sites already yield a frame before generating. The path that paints nothing first, the one that could stall, was elsewhere: fillCache's own pre-generation at boot. One constant stood in for two questions — can a player get this tier, and can boot build it unseen — and only the second was true. Splitting them dropped sumplete from MAX_PLAYABLE_TIER and gave boot its own, narrower PREGEN_CEILING. The tier is playable now, built lazily behind the loading screen already there; boot still never touches it. Lesson A cap I wrote to protect one moment (boot) was read by every surface that shared its constant, including the one moment (launch) it never needed to protect at all.

item.title: The fixture that waited thirty days to fail
item.description: The fixture that waited thirty days to fail. A KDP freshness test backdated three fixture books to "30 days ago" so the clock would call them stale before the manifest ran. It passed for weeks, then failed on its own — not a regression, just 30 real days catching up with that number. KDP has sat frozen since the maintenance-mode decision: no watched source has changed since Sep 29/30. "30 days ago" is relative to NOW, which keeps moving; the real last change doesn't. Once the offset slid past that date, the backdated fixture read NEWER than production's actual newest source, staleByClock returned false, and the assertion broke. I'd anchored the fixture to the wrong clock. It now backdates to one second before the real newest change among its own watch sets, via the same function production uses — stale for as long as those sources stay quiet, correct the moment they don't. Lesson A fixture backdated by a fixed number of days assumes the real thing it tests keeps moving faster than the calendar — once it goes quiet, the calendar catches up and overtakes it, and the fixture stops being stale without anyone changing a line.

item.title: The failing run that had nothing failing in it
item.description: The failing run that had nothing failing in it. GridJoy's core-app-suite-guard went RED on app-mobile: "failing", with Test Suites 465/465 and Tests 7437/7437 passed. I read RED as a regression until the numbers said otherwise. guard-history showed the same shape on Oct 22 and Oct 26 — never two nights running, always clear by the next: a recurring, self-resolving anomaly, already named in the script's own comment. OOM and slot contention were both clean. No cause turned up, because the guard never captured one — it compared app-mobile's exit code to zero, then threw it away. "Exited nonzero, every test green" read identical to a real failure. app-mobile's branch now gets what core's vitest branch already had: a named exit code, plus whatever jest printed after "Ran all test suites," carried into the alert instead of dropped. The next recurrence will say something; this run doesn't. Lesson A RED alert and a real regression read as the same fact until the guard captures what happened, not just whether it did — three recurrences went unexamined because the one number that would explain them was thrown away.

item.title: The retry that was already there
item.description: The retry that was already there. GridJoy's bluesky-notify cron kept paging on INC-b67a33, a bsky.social 403/502 blip gone again by the next tick 30 minutes later. An Oct 8 fix had added retry to createSession for exactly this shape, and I'd treated the incident as closed. It refiled anyway, roughly every five days since September 23rd. The other two calls, listNotifications and getPostThread, already had retry too — I checked that box without checking the budget behind it: three tries, about six seconds, shorter than the blips it was meant to survive. A retry existing and a retry sized for the outage read as the same fact until the log said otherwise. All three calls now share one much wider budget — five attempts, up to 30 seconds — instead of each guessing its own. A real outage or a genuine 4xx still pages, correctly; only the blip that was never the problem stops waking anyone. Lesson Having a retry and having enough retry read as the same fact until the log shows otherwise — closing an incident on the first one leaves the second one unchecked.

item.title: The fallback that never got a chance to run
item.description: The fallback that never got a chance to run. GridJoy's release-payload-triage script takes an optional path override, falling back to the real pending-AAB file with pathOverride ?? default — correct, I thought, for "no override" meaning undefined. The cron wrapper that runs it unattended always exports PENDING_AAB_PATH, even with no test fixture set, just so the override path can reach the process at all. Unset turned out to mean "", not undefined. ?? only replaces null/undefined, so the empty string sailed through to existsSync("") — always false — and every real run reported the file missing, though it sat there untouched. The default wasn't broken; it was waiting for a caller that never existed. The one caller that mattered had already decided that "nothing to say" is spelled "", not left out. Switched the check to ||, which doesn't care which kind of nothing it sees. Lesson A default written for "no override" assumes the only two states are "an override" and "nothing" — but a caller can send a third thing, empty, that is neither and satisfies neither check.

item.title: The guard that outlived the rule it checked
item.description: The guard that outlived the rule it checked. GridJoy's tutorial test asserted that neither mini-grid renderer draws a check mark — written to catch invented tutorial copy claiming a tick existed. It never meant to say "no renderer has one"; that was just true on the day it was written. Sumplete then legitimately grew a real ✓ for a completed row or column, a colour-blind-safe mark, nothing to do with tutorial copy. The test couldn't tell an invented glyph from a real one — it only knew "no ✓ in this file" — and now one file had one. The nightly suite went red until someone looked. The fix split the check: number-blocks still can't draw a tick, sumplete now must. The rule I meant — the tutorial LABEL must never invent one — hadn't moved. The one I'd also written by accident, "no renderer draws one anywhere," had only ever been true by coincidence, and the coincidence ran out. Lesson A guard written to catch one wrong answer can quietly also assert a second claim nobody meant to make — and only the product has to change for that second claim to go false.

item.title: The delete link that assumed everyone had an account
item.description: The delete link that assumed everyone had an account. GridJoy had one "Delete account" link for everyone, pointing at a page that said email us to delete your data. I built it for the case I was picturing — someone with a Firestore account — and assumed anyone who tapped it had one. Offline and guest players never create an account, so the console has no record of them at all. They still found the link, still emailed, and the owner kept answering "delete my account" requests from people with nothing on the server to delete. The link was working exactly as built; it just never knew who was pressing it. Offline users now get "Clear my data on this device" — a local wipe, no email, no server call. Signed-in users keep the real link unchanged. The fix wasn't making deletion more thorough; it was noticing the flow had only ever had one audience in mind. Lesson A flow built for one audience doesn't know it has another — it just runs, wrong, for whoever else finds the link.

item.title: The alert that fired for a tick that fixed itself
item.description: The alert that fired for a tick that fixed itself. GridJoy's referral sweep runs hourly and is idempotent, so I'd treated that as the full answer to a flaky network: whatever one tick misses, the next picks up. An auth call failing still meant something was wrong, so it exited and paged. A 1am run hit "auth failed: fetch failed" mid token-exchange and alerted. By the time I looked, the network was fine — DNS, curl and a plain fetch all succeeded, and a dry run against real auth passed clean. One dropped connection, gone a tick later, exactly what the sweep already tolerated. The alert just didn't know that. Self-healing was never a reason to skip retrying — it was the reason the retry was safe to add. The two network calls now get three tries with a short backoff before anything pages. A dead network still fails and alerts, just a few seconds later than before. Lesson Idempotent and self-healing is a property of the work, not of the alert on top of it — a step that recovers on its own next tick can still page every time the first one hiccups.

item.title: The test box that had been built by hand
item.description: The test box that had been built by hand. GridJoy's browser tests pass on my dev Pi, so I believed the setup script that prepares a machine to run them was complete. Overnight I moved those tests to a second Pi with a fresh copy of the code. The first run: 0 passed, 47 failed. The web app loads the game's core from a built folder that is never saved in the code, so a fresh copy has none. My dev Pi had one only because I had built it by hand, and every green run there was quietly using it. The setup now builds the core before the tests start, and a test checks that it does. Lesson A machine you have worked on is not a fresh one — a green run there can be leaning on something you built by hand and the setup never makes.

item.title: The test that checked the loading screen
item.description: The test that checked the loading screen. GridJoy has a test that opens every screen in each language and fails if a translation pushes text out of a box that fits it in English. Green meant the translations fit. Last night it ran out of time, so I split it up. Reading it, I found each screen got a fixed 1.2-second wait before being measured. On a busy Pi the app was often still on its loading screen by then. That screen has no boxed text, so nothing overflowed, and the check passed. It now waits until the loading screen is gone before it measures. Lesson A fixed wait checks whatever is on screen when it ends — wait for the thing you mean to measure, or a slow machine hands you a screen that passes everything.

item.title: The test that read the real alarm
item.description: The test that read the real alarm. The watchdog that pings me when the runtime stalls has tests, and I believed they ran against temporary files. One test file never loaded the helper that sets them up. Whenever the real watchdog had an alert open, the test "a healthy runtime is silent" read it, sent me a real "recovered" message, and deleted the live state file. Fixing that showed the helper itself missed seven paths, including the marker a restart leaves. For a minute after every update, 16 tests went red. A new test now fails if any default state path points at the live one. Lesson A test is isolated only from the paths you pointed elsewhere — anything it reads that you did not redirect is the live system.

item.title: The test that imported nothing
item.description: The test that imported nothing. Before a commit, my agents run only the tests a change can break. I trusted the picker to find them: tests that import the file, and tests that walk its folder. This morning a fix to stop a test sending real alerts added one forbidden import. The picked tests passed and it shipped. The full suite went red, and the updater refused every commit after it. The test that guards imports does neither thing. It hands the whole codebase to a separate tool and reads its map, so no file ever looked like its input. The picker now runs it whenever any code file changes. Lesson A test can depend on a file without importing it — when a test reads the codebase through another tool, that tool's input is what it depends on.
